title: Metadata and Ontologies
answer: Metadata and ontologies in research data and repositories cover the structured descriptions that make data, papers, models, and tools discoverable and the formal vocabularies that give those descriptions shared meaning. Metadata records typically include title, creator, date, format, identifier, rights, and provenance, while ontologies define classes, properties, and relationships for a domain. Together they support citation, interoperability, reproducibility, and semantic search across repositories. A glossary of 686 terms is a controlled vocabulary, and a full ontology would add relationships and logical rules on top of those terms.

sections.body: Metadata and ontologies in research data and repositories cover the structured descriptions that make data, papers, models, and tools discoverable and the formal vocabularies that give those descriptions shared meaning. Together they support citation, interoperability, reproducibility, and semantic search across repositories. A glossary of 686 terms is a controlled vocabulary, and a full ontology would add relationships and logical rules on top of those terms.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: This work runs on repository platforms, metadata schemas, and identifier systems. Common building blocks include Dublin Core, DataCite, schema.org, RDF, OWL, SKOS, JSON-LD, and SPARQL endpoints. Persistent identifiers such as DOI, ORCID, and ROR anchor records to people, organisations, and objects. Storage may be a relational catalogue, a triple store, or a search index, with validation services checking records against profiles.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners create metadata by hand, by automated extraction, or by mapping existing records to a target schema, then validate and version the result. Ontology work usually starts with competency questions, reuses existing vocabularies where possible, and defines classes, properties, and axioms in an editor such as Protégé. Automated extraction from papers can produce structured claims, and each claim needs provenance metadata such as source, method, and confidence. Human review checks accuracy, resolves conflicts, and records decisions so later users can trace how a term or record changed.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area turn on accurate provenance, clear licences, and controlled vocabulary change. Metadata records carry access conditions, rights holders, licences, and the chain of custody for each object. Ontologies need versioning, deprecation notes, and governance for who may add or alter terms, because biased or unstable vocabularies can distort discovery and analysis. This site links to original papers rather than to a search tool, which keeps provenance tied to the source and avoids an intermediary layer in the citation record.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward machine-actionable metadata, knowledge graphs, and closer alignment between repository catalogues and domain ontologies. FAIR and CARE principles are shaping expectations for findability, access, interoperability, reuse, and Indigenous data governance. Automated extraction and large language models will help populate metadata and suggest ontology mappings, but human curation and provenance remain essential. Future work will likely focus on modular ontologies, cross-repository identifiers, and transparent credit for the people and systems that create metadata.
